title: We Are Not Friends, We Are Not Family — We Are a Team
summary: Personal relationships must never become more important than the client, the team, the standard, fairness, accountability, or job responsibilities. At work, we are a professional team.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, therapists may naturally develop friendships, emotional connections, and close relationships with one another. Some colleagues may become very close outside work.
However, the workplace must remain a professional environment.
When we say "We are not friends, we are not family here at work — we are a team," we are not saying therapists should be cold, distant, hostile, or uncaring.

We are establishing an important professional boundary: Personal relationships must never become more important than the client, the team, the standard, fairness, accountability, or the responsibilities of the job.
At work, the relationship that matters operationally is TEAM MEMBER TO TEAM MEMBER.
A team exists because people have a shared responsibility and shared objective, even when they have different personalities, relationships, opinions, backgrounds, or levels of closeness.
At Zura Spa, our shared objective is: To work together professionally and consistently to deliver an exceptional Zura Spa experience to every client.

sections.title: 1. Why This Standard Matters
paragraphs: A workplace built primarily around friendship can easily become a workplace where friends protect friends, people form cliques, rules apply differently depending on relationships, corrections become personal, personal disagreements affect work, some people feel excluded, leaders become afraid to correct people close to them, team members hide one another's mistakes, and personal loyalty becomes stronger than loyalty to the standard.
Zura Spa cannot operate effectively that way.

A professional team must be able to say: "I care about you personally, but I still need you to follow the standard." "We are close, but I cannot hide this mistake." "We had a disagreement, but we still have a client to serve."
That is maturity.

sections.title: 2. The Therapist's Mindset
paragraphs: Every therapist should have the mindset: "I can care about my colleagues without allowing personal relationships to interfere with my professionalism."
Friendship is optional. Respect is required. Cooperation is required. Accountability is required. Professional conduct is required.

You do not need to personally like everyone you work with. You do need to respect them, communicate appropriately, support their work where required, honour professional boundaries, perform shared responsibilities, and treat them fairly.

sections.title: 3. What Being a Team Means
paragraphs: Being a team means the following principles.

sections.title: We Support, But We Do Not Cover Up
paragraphs: If a colleague is struggling, support them. If they make a mistake, help them correct it.
But do not lie, hide information, or protect misconduct because the person is your friend.

sections.title: We Communicate, But We Do Not Gossip
paragraphs: If there is a problem, communicate with the person involved or escalate through the appropriate channel. Do not build alliances around complaints.

sections.title: We Correct, But We Do Not Humiliate
paragraphs: Team members should be able to respectfully remind one another of standards. Correction should be professional, not insulting.

sections.title: We Care, But We Maintain Boundaries
paragraphs: You can care about a colleague's wellbeing without becoming responsible for their finances, personal decisions, emotional stability, belongings, or work responsibilities.
Support should not become dependency.

sections.title: We Work Together, But We Remain Accountable Individually
paragraphs: A shared assignment does not remove individual responsibility.
If your part was not done, saying "But we were doing it together" does not automatically remove accountability.

sections.title: We Can Disagree Without Becoming Enemies
paragraphs: Professional disagreement should not become silent treatment, gossip, retaliation, refusal to cooperate, sabotage, or cliques.

sections.title: We Put the Client Above Personal Feelings
paragraphs: If two therapists have a personal disagreement and are assigned together, the client should not experience the disagreement.
The client did not come to manage staff relationships.

sections.title: 4. Friendship Must Not Affect Accountability
paragraphs: A friend may break something, miss a task, flout a standard, mishandle a client, fail to give a report, or make an operational mistake.
The fact that the person is your friend does not change what should happen.
If the matter requires reporting, report it. If correction is necessary, correct it. If escalation is necessary, escalate it.
Protect the person through truth and correction, not through concealment.
Covering up repeated poor behaviour does not actually help the colleague. It allows the problem to grow.

sections.title: 5. Friendship Must Not Affect Leadership
paragraphs: A leader may be personally close to some therapists. That friendship must not determine assignments, corrections, opportunities, assessments, enforcement of standards, access to information, discipline, recognition, or work expectations.
Leaders must be able to say: "We may be friends outside work, but I must handle this fairly in my leadership role."
Friendship cannot become immunity from accountability.

sections.title: 6. Personal Disagreements Must Not Affect Work
paragraphs: Two therapists may disagree personally. That does not give either person permission to refuse to work together, withhold information, ignore task updates, refuse to support a co-therapist, deliberately reduce massage synchronization, avoid necessary communication, sabotage another person's work, or bring hostility into the massage room.
Professional responsibility continues even when personal feelings are uncomfortable.
The correct mindset is: "I may not be happy with you right now, but I will still perform my responsibility professionally."

sections.title: 7. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite of this standard is a workplace operating like a friendship circle instead of a professional team.

sections.title: Cliques
paragraphs: Small groups form and begin operating as "Us versus them." Information, support, and relationships become controlled by friendship groups.

sections.title: Favouritism
paragraphs: Friends receive more support, easier treatment, better opportunities, fewer corrections, and special exceptions. Others notice and begin losing trust in the system.

sections.title: Covering Up
paragraphs: A therapist sees their friend flout a standard, damage property, mishandle a task, or make a serious mistake, but stays silent because "That is my person." This damages accountability.

sections.title: Selective Reporting
paragraphs: A therapist reports people they are not close to but protects close friends. This makes the reporting system unfair.

sections.title: Friendship-Based Loyalty
paragraphs: A therapist believes: "If you're my friend, you should always support me, even when I'm wrong." That is not professional loyalty.

sections.title: Taking Correction Personally
paragraphs: A colleague gives professional feedback and the response becomes: "I thought we were friends." Friendship does not remove professional correction.

sections.title: Personal Conflict Entering Work
paragraphs: A private disagreement leads to coldness, refusal to cooperate, withholding assistance, poor handover, tension during massage, or gossip. This is unacceptable.

sections.title: Exclusion
paragraphs: Friendship groups may deliberately leave others out, ignore certain people, withhold information, or mock outsiders. That creates an unsafe workplace.

sections.title: 8. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate a Friendship-Based Work Culture
paragraphs: A friendship-based workplace creates inconsistent standards.

The business begins depending on who likes who, who is close to leadership, who belongs to which group, and who protects whom — instead of standards, responsibilities, performance, fairness, and accountability.

Zura Spa will therefore not normalize cliques, favouritism, cover-ups, personal alliances against colleagues, retaliation after disagreements, friendship being used to avoid accountability, leaders treating friends differently, staff withholding support because of personal conflict, exclusion, or group pressure.
The workplace must remain safe and fair even for someone who is not personally close to anybody.

sections.title: 9. Impact on the Team
paragraphs: A friendship-based culture creates division, suspicion, unequal accountability, difficulty correcting, gossip, and can make new therapists feel unsafe.
Once people identify primarily as friendship groups, the team stops functioning as one unit.
People begin asking: "Was she treated differently because they are friends?" Trust in leadership and fairness reduces.
One person's mistake is reported. Another person's mistake is hidden. That destroys confidence in standards.
People begin viewing professional feedback as betrayal. This prevents growth.
Friend groups often become places where complaints about other colleagues are discussed. That creates misunderstanding and resentment.

A new therapist entering a workplace full of established friendship circles may feel isolated, unwelcome, unsupported, or unable to speak. The team should not require social membership before someone feels respected.

If two therapists are personally upset with one another, the client may notice poor communication, bad synchronization, tension, silence, or lack of support. Internal relationships must never become a client's problem.

sections.title: 10. What Healthy Team Relationships Look Like
paragraphs: A healthy Zura Spa team can laugh together, support one another, celebrate one another, care about each other's wellbeing, enjoy working together, and build genuine friendships.
But it can also correct each other, report problems, say no, maintain boundaries, disagree, hold each other accountable, and work fairly with people outside their friendship circle.
That balance is the standard.

sections.title: 11. Teamwork Does Not Mean Personal Dependence
paragraphs: Being a team does not mean "Everything I need, my colleagues should provide."
Each therapist is still expected to be independent, responsible, prepared, disciplined, and accountable.

The team supports professional work. The team should not become the primary system through which an individual manages money, food, personal belongings, emotional responsibilities, or personal obligations.
This aligns with the Zura Spa No-Borrowing and Personal Independence Standard.

sections.title: 12. Teamwork and Reporting
paragraphs: Being a team means important information should not be hidden to protect relationships.
If a report is required: report to the appropriate leader, use the appropriate WhatsApp wall where required, give the facts, protect confidentiality, and avoid gossip.
My responsibility is to the team and the standard, not to protecting a private alliance.

sections.title: 13. Teamwork and Task Execution
paragraphs: If a task is assigned: know your role, complete your responsibility, support others where appropriate, give Task Completion Report, allow Task Review, correct where necessary, and close the task.
Do not expect a friend to cover your missed task, give a false update, take responsibility for your mistake, or protect you from review.

sections.title: 14. What Therapists Should Do
list: Work professionally with people they are not personally close to.
Separate personal relationships from work decisions.
Continue performing responsibilities even during personal disagreement.
Welcome new therapists into the team.
Follow the same standards regardless of friendship.
Put client experience ahead of personal feelings.

sections.title: 15. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Expect friends to lie for them.
Become angry because a friend corrected them.
Say, "I thought we were friends," to avoid accountability.
Refuse to work with someone after a disagreement.
Stop supporting a co-therapist professionally because of personal issues.
Gossip about colleagues inside friendship groups.
Use leadership friendships to seek special treatment.
Mock therapists who are not part of a social group.
Allow personal disagreement to affect clients.
Treat someone badly simply because you are not friends.

sections.title: 16. Leaders Have a Higher Responsibility
paragraphs: Managers, SMs, CMs, SPs, LTs and TGs must be especially careful.
Leadership must not create a perception that friends receive special treatment, fewer corrections, better assignments, protection, or that rules depend on relationships.
Leaders should be approachable and caring while remaining fair.
The leadership mindset should be: "I may have personal relationships, but my decisions at work must be professional, explainable and consistent with the standard."

sections.title: 17. You Do Not Need to Like Someone to Work Well With Them
paragraphs: This is an important professional skill.
A therapist may honestly think: "Thr. Jane is not someone I would personally choose as a friend." That is acceptable.
But if assigned together, both therapists should still speak respectfully, communicate, synchronize, support one another, complete tasks, and protect the client's experience.
Professional cooperation does not require personal friendship.

sections.title: 18. Correction and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: Becoming friends with colleagues = acceptable. Supporting a friend professionally = healthy teamwork. Having a personal disagreement + continuing to work professionally = maturity. Correcting a friend respectfully = accountability.

But: Covering up a friend's mistake = accountability concern. Favouritism based on friendship = professional conduct concern. Forming cliques that affect work = team culture concern. Retaliating against someone after personal conflict = serious conduct concern. Deliberately allowing friendship to override client safety or standards = serious accountability concern.

sections.title: 19. The Zura Spa Team Standard
paragraphs: RESPECT → SUPPORT → COMMUNICATE → ACCOUNT → CORRECT → COOPERATE → PROTECT THE STANDARD

Every therapist should regularly ask: Am I treating this person fairly, or differently because of friendship? Would I respond the same way if another therapist did this? Am I protecting a colleague or covering up a problem? Has personal disagreement affected my professional behaviour? Can I receive correction without turning it into a friendship issue? Can I professionally work with someone I do not personally like? Is the client experiencing any consequence of our personal relationships?
WE ARE NOT REQUIRED TO BE FRIENDS. WE ARE NOT A FAMILY SYSTEM AT WORK. WE ARE A PROFESSIONAL TEAM.

We support without covering up. We care without creating unhealthy dependence. We communicate without gossip. We disagree without becoming enemies. We correct without disrespect. We maintain boundaries without becoming cold. We work together without losing individual accountability.
We build friendships where they naturally develop, but friendship never becomes more important than the Zura Spa standard.
At work, the standard comes before the friendship, the client comes before personal feelings, and the team comes before the clique.
WE SUCCEED TOGETHER. WE REMAIN ACCOUNTABLE INDIVIDUALLY. WE PROTECT THE ZURA SPA STANDARD TOGETHER.

remember: At work we are a professional team. Friendship never becomes more important than the standard, the client, or fairness.
